Most people meet the *Book of Documents* (尚书) as a pile of archaic royal speeches. I have been reading it the other way round: as a working manual of governance, one chapter at a time, and publishing a full annotated edition at [daokedao-shangshu](https://q1z2q3-debug.github.io/daokedao-shangshu/). This is the first of a series.

## What the text actually says

The Canon of Yao opens with sixteen characters that read like a programme:

> 克明俊德，以亲九族。九族既睦，平章百姓。百姓昭明，协和万邦，黎民于变时雍。
>
> He clarified his own great virtue, and thereby brought harmony to his nine kin-clans. When the nine clans were at peace, he distinguished and illuminated the hundred clans. When the hundred clans shone, he harmonised the myriad states — and the common people, transformed, became serene.

Four layers, in order: oneself, one's kin, the officials, the states, the people. No layer may be skipped.

## Three things worth stealing from it

**1. Sequence is the argument.** Modern reform fails less often on direction than on order: the slogan is aimed at the furthest ring while the nearest ring — one's own conduct, one's own household, the three people one actually works with — is left hollow. The text puts self-clarification first, and treats the rest as deductions, not as parallel slogans.

**2. Calendar before administration.** Yao's second act is to appoint Xi and He to "reverently deliver the seasons to the people": observe the sun, moon and stars, fix the four seasons, intercalate a month so that the year comes out right (the text says 366 days). Only then does the machinery of officials begin. Agricultural work, corvée, sacrifice, campaign — each has its season. To schedule people's labour without knowing the rhythm is to work against time.

**3. Doubt stays inside the procedure.** When Yao asks for candidates, Fangqi proposes his own son; Yao answers that the man is quarrelsome. Huandou proposes Gonggong; Yao answers that he talks well and acts crookedly. The Four Mountains propose Gun for the floods; Yao says he will ruin the clans, yet still tests him for nine years, and Gun fails. Finally Shun, from a humble and obscure place, is brought forward — and Yao marries two daughters to him to watch his household discipline, then tests him with the five constants, the hundred duties, the reception of guests, the four mountains, the lords.

Raise, doubt, test, observe. Reputation is only a lead; performance is the proof. The crowd's voice, however loud, does not get to erase the doubt. **Keep the doubt in the procedure, not in personal relations** — that is the single most practical line in the chapter.

## The handover

After seventy years in office Yao asks to step down: "Exalt the bright, and raise those in obscure places." Even the hidden and the lowly are to be brought up; office is not passed to kin. The chapter does not stage a grand abdication scene. It records consultation, testing, observation. Which tells you something: for these writers, handing over power was hard — hard enough that it had to be walked through as a procedure.

## One practice

Before pushing a distant goal this week, check the nearest ring: your own conduct, your own household, the three people you work with most. If that ring is hollow, the distant promise will come back and hit you.
